short: A plan setting out what a new hire should learn, contribute and own in their first 30, 60 and 90 days.
detail: Share it on day one and use it again at the probation review.

short: Feedback on a person collected from their manager, peers, direct reports and sometimes customers, alongside their own self-rating.
detail: It is most useful for development; tying it directly to pay tends to make the feedback less honest.

short: A rule of thumb that most learning at work comes from experience (70%), some from other people (20%) and a little from formal training (10%).
detail: The proportions are a guide rather than precise research findings, but the idea holds: build learning into real work, not only courses.

short: When an employee stops coming to work for a long period without notice or explanation.
detail: Employers usually send written notices asking the employee to return or explain before treating the job as abandoned. Dues already earned are still payable.

short: Unplanned absence from work, often measured as days absent divided by scheduled working days.
A statement on the income-tax portal listing the income, TDS, tax paid and large transactions reported against your PAN.
detail: Check it against your Form 16 (Form 130 from tax year 2026-27) before filing your return; for years up to 2025-26, TDS credits also appear in Form 26AS.

short: The formal letter that confirms your employment and its terms, such as designation, wages, hours and benefits.
detail: Under the OSH Code, every employee must get one on joining, in the format the rules prescribe; it is a legal duty, not just good practice. Existing employees without one were due to receive it within three months of the Code taking effect, that is by February 2026.

short: The formal review of your performance over a period, usually a year, which often feeds into your rating, increment and promotion.
detail: A fair appraisal uses evidence from the whole period, not just the last few months, and includes your own self-assessment.

short: Whichever government, central or state, is responsible for applying a labour law to a particular establishment.
detail: For most private businesses it is the state government, so state rules decide many details such as minimum wages and forms.

short: Pay that was due for an earlier period but is paid later, for example when a pay rise is backdated.
detail: Arrears are taxed in the year you receive them. If that pushes you into a higher tax slab, you may be able to claim relief when you file your return.

short: Software that collects job applications and tracks each candidate through the hiring stages.
detail: It holds candidates' personal data, so access, retention and consent should follow the DPDP Act as its duties come into force.

short: A request in the HR system to correct your attendance record, for example after a missed punch, field work or a day working from home.
detail: Your manager usually approves it. Absences left unregularised can be treated as loss of pay, so fix them before the payroll cut-off.

short: People leaving an organisation, usually measured as exits in a period divided by average headcount.
detail: Track voluntary and involuntary exits separately, and look at who is leaving, not just how many.

short: Checks an employer runs, often through an agency, to confirm a candidate's identity, education and past jobs, and sometimes address or criminal record.
detail: Tell candidates what will be checked and get their consent, since it involves personal data. Offers are often made 'subject to background verification'.

short: The fixed core part of your salary, on which items such as HRA and PF are often calculated.
detail: Basic pay and dearness allowance always count as 'wages' under the Labour Codes. A low basic no longer cuts PF and gratuity the way it used to, because most other allowances also count as wages and excluded ones above half your pay are added back.

short: A rating method that makes managers place set proportions of employees in each rating, such as a fixed share at the top and bottom.
detail: It can curb rating inflation, but in small or high-performing teams it forces unfair low ratings, so many companies use calibration instead.

short: Any payment over and above your regular salary, such as a festival, performance or joining bonus.
detail: Statutory bonus is the only kind the law requires; other bonuses depend on your contract and company policy.

short: A meeting in which managers compare proposed ratings across teams so the same standard is applied to everyone.
detail: HR usually runs it, and managers should bring evidence for each rating.

short: Short paid leave for unplanned personal needs, usually taken a day or two at a time.
detail: No national law sets a minimum for private employers; it comes from state Shops and Establishments Acts and company policy (Maharashtra's Act, for example, gives 8 days a year). Unused casual leave usually lapses at the end of the year.

short: The most senior HR leader in an organisation, responsible for people strategy and usually part of the leadership team.
The Labour Code on PF, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit and social security for gig and platform workers.
detail: It replaced nine laws, including the EPF Act, the ESI Act, the Payment of Gratuity Act and the Maternity Benefit Act. The schemes made under the old laws are being reissued under it.

short: The Labour Code on minimum wages, timely payment of wages, bonus and equal pay.
detail: It replaced four older laws, including the Payment of Wages Act and the Minimum Wages Act. Its rules on paying wages on time and on deductions now cover every employee, whatever their salary.

short: A team of HR specialists in one area, such as rewards, talent or learning, who design policies and programmes for the whole company.
A day off you get in place of a weekly off or holiday on which you worked.
detail: Some laws require a substitute holiday when a worker loses the weekly day off or works on a festival holiday; beyond that, company policy sets the rules, including how soon you must use it.

short: Your salary divided by the midpoint of your salary band, showing whether you are paid below, at or above the target for your level.
detail: A compa-ratio of 1.0 means you are at the midpoint. HR teams use it when deciding increments and to spot people who are underpaid.

short: A skill, area of knowledge or behaviour needed to do a job well, such as problem-solving or stakeholder management.
detail: A competency framework describes these for each level, so hiring, appraisal and development use the same yardstick.

short: Settling a minor labour-law offence by paying a set amount instead of being prosecuted.
detail: Under the Labour Codes, many first offences punishable only with a fine can be compounded by paying half the maximum fine. It is not available for a repeat of the same offence within a set period, five years under the Code on Wages.

short: The list in India's Constitution of subjects on which both Parliament and state legislatures can make laws; labour is one of them.
detail: That is why central Labour Codes sit alongside state laws such as the Shops and Establishments Acts, and why the rules differ from state to state.

short: The formal end of probation, when you become a permanent employee, usually stated in a letter.
detail: If performance is not yet where it should be, probation may be extended for a set period, with the reasons given in writing.

short: A person's clear, informed agreement to their personal data being used for a stated purpose.
detail: Under the DPDP Act, whose main duties apply from May 2027, consent must be free, specific and as easy to withdraw as to give. The Act also lets employers use some employee data for employment purposes without consent, but they must still protect it.

short: Workers supplied by a contractor or staffing firm who work at your premises but are on the contractor's payroll.
detail: Under the OSH Code, a contractor employing 50 or more contract workers needs a licence. The principal employer must make sure wages and welfare are provided if the contractor fails.

short: An allowance towards your travel between home and work.
detail: It is one of the items left out of 'wages' under the Labour Codes, subject to the 50% rule, and is generally taxed as part of your salary.

short: The average cost of filling a role: total recruiting spend in a period divided by the number of hires.
detail: Include agency fees, job boards, referral bonuses, tools and recruiter time.

short: An offer from your current employer, usually more pay, to persuade you to stay after you resign.
detail: Before accepting, revisit why you wanted to leave; more pay rarely fixes those reasons on its own.

short: A day-care facility for employees' young children at or near the workplace.
detail: Under the Code on Social Security, establishments with 50 or more employees must provide a crèche for children under six, on their own or shared with others, and allow the mother four visits a day. The Central Rules make it available to employees of any gender.

short: The total yearly cost of employing you, including salary, bonuses and employer contributions you never see in your bank account.
detail: CTC usually includes the employer's PF share, a gratuity provision and insurance, so your in-hand pay is always lower than CTC divided by 12. Compare offers on fixed pay and in-hand pay, not CTC alone.

short: An organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed; an employer is the data fiduciary for its employees' data.
detail: It stays responsible even when a vendor, such as a payroll provider, processes the data on its behalf.

short: The person the personal data is about, such as a job applicant or an employee.
detail: Data principals have rights to access, correct, update and erase their data, and to nominate someone to act for them.

short: The body set up under the DPDP Act to inquire into personal data breaches and complaints and to impose penalties.
detail: The provisions setting it up came into force in November 2025, ahead of most of the Act.

short: An allowance that adjusts pay for rising prices, common in government jobs and in minimum wages.
detail: It counts as 'wages' under the Labour Codes, so it affects PF, gratuity and bonus. Most private-sector salaries do not have a separate DA, but minimum wage rates often include a variable dearness allowance that states revise from time to time.

short: An internal hearing to decide whether an employee committed the misconduct alleged against them.
detail: An impartial inquiry officer hears both sides, lets the employee answer the evidence and records findings. Dismissals made without this step are easy to challenge.

short: India's law on how organisations collect, use, store and share people's digital personal data, including an employer's handling of employee data.
detail: The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025 with an 18-month phase-in, so most duties, such as notices, security safeguards and breach reporting, apply from May 2027. Until then, the older IT Act rules on sensitive personal data still apply.

short: The central government's portal for registering unorganised, gig and platform workers so they can reach social security schemes.
detail: Registration is free and Aadhaar-based, and each registered worker gets a unique number.

short: Paid leave you build up as you work, which you can plan in advance, carry forward and often encash.
detail: Under the OSH Code, a worker who works 180 days or more in a calendar year earns one day for every 20 days worked, can carry forward up to 30 days and can encash unused leave. State Shops and Establishments Acts and company policy may be more generous.

short: The monthly online return an employer files with EPFO to report and pay each employee's PF contributions.
detail: It is due by the 15th of the following month. Wrong wages or missing UANs in the ECR are a common reason employees' PF balances look wrong.

short: Life insurance that comes with your PF membership, paid for by your employer, which pays your family if you die while in service.
detail: You pay nothing towards it. The payout depends on your wages and PF balance, within limits set by the scheme.

short: How committed people feel to their work and organisation, and how much effort they choose to put in.
detail: It is usually measured through surveys; what matters is acting on the results team by team.

short: The stages a person goes through with an employer: attract, hire, onboard, develop, retain and exit.
A candidate recommended by a current employee, often with a referral bonus paid if they are hired.
detail: Referrals tend to be quicker and cheaper to hire, but relying on them alone can make a team less diverse.

short: How a company is seen as a place to work, and the work of shaping that reputation.
detail: Honest employee stories, prompt replies to candidates and fair treatment of people who leave do more than advertising.

short: A score based on how likely employees are, on a scale of 0 to 10, to recommend their workplace.
detail: It is the percentage of promoters (9 or 10) minus the percentage of detractors (0 to 6), so it runs from −100 to +100.

short: A retirement savings fund, run by EPFO, into which you and your employer each pay a share of your wages every month.
detail: Establishments with 20 or more employees must cover staff, with 12% of PF wages from each side. From 17 September 2026, membership is compulsory for employees earning up to {{fact:epf.wageCeiling}} at joining, and those above can join with the employer's agreement.

short: The pension scheme run by EPFO that pays you a monthly pension after retirement, funded from part of your employer's PF contribution.
detail: {{fact:epf.epsRate}} of your wages, up to the PF wage ceiling, goes to the pension account instead of your PF balance. The EPF, EPS and EDLI schemes were reissued under the Code on Social Security in June 2026.

short: The rule that employers may not pay people differently for the same or similar work because of their gender.
detail: The Code on Wages also bars gender discrimination in recruitment and conditions of work, and expressly covers transgender persons.

short: A government health insurance scheme for lower-paid employees that covers medical care and pays cash during sickness, maternity and injury.
detail: It applies in establishments with 10 or more employees, now anywhere in India, to employees earning up to {{fact:esi.wageCeiling}} ({{fact:esi.wageCeilingPwd|short}} for persons with disability); the employee pays a small share of wages and the employer a larger one. ESI rules are being reissued under the Code on Social Security, so check current figures in the ESI calculator.

short: A plan that gives employees the option to buy company shares later at a fixed price.
detail: Options vest over time, often after a one-year 'cliff', and you must exercise them within a set window. They are taxed as a perquisite when you exercise and again as capital gains when you sell.

short: The reasons a good person would choose to join and stay, such as pay, growth, the work itself, culture and flexibility.
A payment made as goodwill rather than as a legal duty, such as a festival payment or a lump sum on exit.
detail: Ex gratia paid on termination is left out of 'wages' under the Labour Codes. Some employers pay it to staff who earn too much to qualify for statutory bonus.

short: A conversation or survey with a departing employee to understand why they are leaving and what could be better.
detail: Keep answers confidential and look for patterns across exits rather than reacting to single comments.

short: The salary you ask for in a new job; recruiters in India usually ask for your current CTC as well.
detail: Give a range based on the market rate for the role, not just a percentage rise on your current pay. Employers should pay for the role rather than anchor on your last salary.

short: A letter stating your role and period of employment, which you can show future employers.
detail: It is often combined with the relieving letter.

short: Employment on a written contract for a set period, which ends when the period is over.
detail: Under the IR Code, fixed-term employees must get the same hours, wages, allowances and benefits as permanent staff doing the same work, and gratuity after one year. A contract simply ending on its date is not retrenchment.

short: A national minimum pay level set by the central government, below which no state may fix its minimum wages.
detail: The Code on Wages lets the Centre set it, after consulting the states, and it can differ by region. Check the latest notification before relying on a figure.

short: The declaration a mid-year joiner gives the new employer, showing salary and TDS from the previous job in the same year.
detail: Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 it is Form 122, which also replaces Form 12BAA for declaring other income and house-property loss. Without it, your new employer may deduct too little tax and you may face a demand when you file your return.

short: A statement from your employer listing your perks, such as a company car or stock options, and the taxable value of each.
detail: Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 it is Form 123.

short: The form you give your employer to claim HRA, LTA, home-loan interest and tax-saving investments, so they are counted in your monthly TDS.
detail: Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 it is Form 124. Attach proof, and give your landlord's PAN if your rent is more than ₹1,00,000 a year; most of these claims matter only if you choose the old tax regime.

short: The yearly certificate your employer gives you showing the salary paid and the tax deducted from it.
detail: Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 it is Form 130, issued for each tax year from 2026-27 by 15 June after the year ends. It shows the tax deposited against your PAN and how your salary and tax were worked out, so check it against your AIS before filing your return.

short: The quarterly return in which an employer reports the salary paid and the TDS deducted for each employee.
detail: Under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 it is Form 138. Your TDS shows against your PAN only after this return is filed correctly.

short: The last payment when you leave, covering unpaid salary, leave encashment, bonus and other dues, minus any recoveries.
detail: Under the Code on Wages, wages due must be paid within two working days of resignation, removal, dismissal or retrenchment, commonly counted from the last working day. Gratuity follows within 30 days of becoming payable, so company policies that allow 30 to 45 days need updating.

short: Part of a notice period during which you stay employed and paid but are asked not to work or contact clients.
detail: It is purely contractual. Courts are more willing to enforce restrictions during employment, including garden leave, than after it ends.

short: The difference between what men and women earn on average, across the whole organisation or at the same level.
detail: An organisation-wide gap often reflects fewer women in senior roles; a gap at the same level and role points to unequal pay. Track both.

short: A person who earns from short-term tasks or projects outside a traditional employer–employee relationship, such as freelance or delivery work.
detail: The Code on Social Security recognises gig and platform workers for the first time and provides for social security schemes for them, partly funded by aggregators. They can register on the e-Shram portal.

short: A lump sum your employer pays when you leave after at least five years of continuous service, as a reward for long service.
detail: It is 15 days' wages for each completed year (monthly wages divided by 26), capped at {{fact:gratuity.ceiling}}, and must be paid within 30 days of becoming due. Fixed-term employees qualify after one year, the five-year rule does not apply on death or disablement, and 'wages' means the Labour Code definition, not just basic pay.

short: A committee of employer and worker representatives that settles individual workers' complaints.
detail: The IR Code requires one in industrial establishments with 20 or more workers, with women represented at least in proportion to their share of the workforce.

short: Your total salary for a month or a year before deductions such as your PF share, professional tax and TDS.
detail: It is roughly CTC minus the employer's own contributions, such as employer PF and gratuity, and minus variable pay not yet earned. Companies define it slightly differently, so check the breakup in your offer.

short: Medical insurance your employer buys for staff, often also covering spouse, children or parents.
detail: Its cost is often shown as part of CTC. Cover usually ends when you leave, so check whether you can move to a personal policy.

short: The number of people employed, either at a point in time or as planned.
detail: Be clear whether it includes contract staff, interns and open roles.

short: An employee judged able to grow into much bigger roles, faster than their peers.
detail: Potential is harder to judge than performance, so use clear criteria and review the list regularly.

short: An allowance in your salary meant to help you pay rent.
detail: Under the old tax regime, part of it can be tax-free if you pay rent, depending on your rent, salary and city; under the new regime it is fully taxable. HRA is one of the items left out of 'wages' under the Labour Codes, subject to the 50% rule.

short: An HR professional assigned to a business unit who advises its leaders on people issues and links HR work to business goals.
detail: HRBPs rely on HR operations for day-to-day processes and on centres of excellence for specialist expertise.

short: Software that stores employee records and supports HR processes such as leave, attendance and payroll.
detail: People often use HRIS and HRMS to mean the same thing; HRMS usually suggests a wider suite.

short: A suite of HR software covering employee records, attendance, leave, payroll, performance and more.
detail: Choose one that handles Indian statutory payroll and lets you control who can see personal data.

short: A plan agreed between you and your manager for the skills and experience you will build, and how.
detail: Good IDPs mix stretch work on the job, coaching and some formal training.

short: The amount that actually reaches your bank account each month after all deductions.
detail: It is gross pay minus your PF share, professional tax, TDS and any other deductions such as unpaid leave. Use the take-home salary calculator to estimate it from your CTC.

short: The law that replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961 on 1 April 2026 and now governs tax on salary.
detail: It works through the Income-tax Rules, 2026, which renumbered most forms: for example, Form 16 became Form 130 and Form 12BB became Form 124.

short: A rise in your salary, usually given once a year after the appraisal.
detail: The percentage usually depends on your rating, where you sit in the salary band and the company's budget. It is confirmed in a salary revision letter.

short: A disagreement between an employer and workers, or among workers, about employment, job loss or terms of work.
detail: Under the IR Code it goes first to conciliation by a government officer; if that does not settle it within 90 days, either side can go to a two-member Industrial Tribunal. A single worker's dispute about dismissal or retrenchment also counts.

short: The Labour Code on trade unions, standing orders, strikes, disputes, lay-offs and retrenchment.
detail: It replaced the Industrial Disputes Act, the Trade Unions Act and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, and it formally recognises fixed-term employment.

short: The labour inspector under the Labour Codes, whose role now includes advising employers on compliance as well as enforcing the law.
detail: For many lapses, employers get a 30-day notice to put things right before prosecution starts.

short: The committee an employer with 10 or more employees must set up to receive and inquire into sexual harassment complaints.
detail: It is led by a senior woman employee, includes an external member from an NGO or with relevant expertise, and at least half its members must be women. A complaint is made within three months of the incident (extendable by three more), and the inquiry must finish within 90 days.

short: The yearly process of telling your employer about rent, investments and other tax claims so your TDS can be adjusted.
detail: You usually declare planned amounts at the start of the tax year and submit proof towards the end; claims without proof are dropped and the extra tax is deducted from your last few salaries. From 1 April 2026 the declaration is made in Form 124.

short: A document that sets out what a role is for, what the person will do and what they need to bring.
detail: A good JD names outcomes and must-have skills, gives a pay range and avoids words that signal a preferred age or gender.

short: A one-time payment to a new hire, often to make up for a bonus or notice buyout they lose by leaving their last job.
detail: Most offers ask you to repay it if you leave within a set period, often a year, so read this clause before you accept.

short: A measurable number used to track performance against a goal, such as sales closed or tickets resolved on time.
detail: Each KRA usually has one to three KPIs, with targets agreed at the start of the review period.

short: One of the main areas of a job where results are expected, such as revenue, quality or team development.
detail: KRAs say where to focus; KPIs measure how well you are doing in each.

short: The four laws that replaced 29 central labour laws on 21 November 2025: the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the OSH Code.
detail: Central rules under all four were notified in May 2026. For most private employers the state government makes the detailed rules, and several states were still finalising them in late 2026, so check the position in your state.

short: A small contribution, from both you and your employer, that some states collect to pay for welfare schemes for workers.
detail: Whether it applies, how much it is and whether it is paid yearly or half-yearly depend on your state's law.

short: The final day you work for an employer before your employment ends.
detail: It follows from your resignation date and notice period, less any buyout or waiver. Your F&F dues are calculated up to this date.

short: In everyday use, job cuts; in the IR Code, a temporary inability to give workers work, for example because of a power or raw-material shortage, while keeping them on the rolls.
detail: Workers on a legal lay-off are paid lay-off compensation, and factories, mines and plantations with 300 or more workers need government permission. Permanent job cuts are retrenchment.

short: Helping employees build skills through training, coaching, mentoring and learning on the job.
detail: Start from the skills the business needs, and check whether behaviour and results change, not just attendance.

short: Being paid cash for earned leave you have not used, during the year or when you leave.
detail: Under the OSH Code, workers can encash unused annual leave at the end of the calendar year, and leave due on leaving is paid within two working days (two months on retirement or death). For other staff, company policy sets how many days can be encashed.

short: The committee set up by the District Officer to handle sexual harassment complaints where there is no Internal Committee or the complaint is against the employer.
detail: It covers workplaces with fewer than 10 employees and women in the unorganised sector, including domestic workers.

short: A deduction from your salary for days you were absent without approved paid leave.
detail: People often use LOP and LWP to mean the same thing; strictly, LWP is approved unpaid leave and LOP is the pay deduction, including for unapproved absence. The Code on Wages allows deductions for absence from duty.

short: An allowance towards the cost of travel within India when you go on leave.
detail: Under the old tax regime, the travel fare can be tax-free for a limited number of journeys if you submit proof; under the new regime LTA is taxable.

short: Approved time off for which you are not paid, usually when your paid leave has run out.
detail: Your pay is cut for each day of LWP, worked out from your monthly pay using the method in your company's policy. Long spells of LWP can also delay increments or confirmation.

short: Paid leave and related benefits for a woman employee around childbirth or adoption.
detail: A woman who has worked at least 80 days in the 12 months before delivery gets up to {{fact:maternity.weeks}} of paid leave, or {{fact:maternity.weeksTwoChildren}} if she already has two or more surviving children; adopting and commissioning mothers get 12 weeks. Since a Supreme Court ruling in March 2026, adoptive mothers qualify whatever the child's age, and the rules now sit in the Code on Social Security.

short: The lowest pay an employer may legally pay for a type of work, fixed by the government for each skill level and area.
detail: Under the Code on Wages it now applies to every employee in every sector, not only to listed 'scheduled employments'. Most rates are set by state governments, which may not fix them below the floor wage.

short: Doing a second paid job or freelance work alongside your main job.
detail: No general law bans it for private-sector office jobs, but your contract or company policy may require permission and will usually forbid working for competitors or using company time and data.

short: Republic Day (26 January), Independence Day (15 August) and Gandhi Jayanti (2 October), the three paid holidays given across India.
detail: State holiday laws add other paid festival holidays, so the total differs by state; Maharashtra, for example, requires 8 a year, including 1 May. Working on one usually earns extra pay or a substitute day off.

short: The default way of working out income tax, with lower slab rates but very few deductions or exemptions.
detail: Your employer deducts TDS under it unless you tell them you want the old regime. Salaried people without business income can choose either regime each year when they file their return.

short: A talent-review grid that places employees by performance on one axis and potential on the other, giving nine boxes.
detail: It helps plan development and succession. Base placements on evidence and discuss them in calibration.

short: Sign-offs from teams such as IT, finance and admin confirming you have returned company property and owe nothing, before your F&F is closed.
detail: Delays in no-dues should not hold up your wages, which the law requires within two working days of leaving.

short: Naming the family members who should receive your PF, gratuity and insurance money if you die.
detail: File your PF nomination on the EPFO portal and your gratuity nomination with your employer soon after joining, and update them after marriage or the birth of a child. Without a valid nomination, your family may face a slow claim process.

short: A clause that stops you working for a competitor or starting a rival business.
detail: In India, restrictions that apply after you leave are generally unenforceable under contract law, but confidentiality duties and restrictions during employment can be enforced. Non-solicitation clauses are judged case by case.

short: Salary paid instead of notice: by the employer when it ends your job without full notice, or by you when you leave without serving it.
detail: If you leave early, the shortfall is usually recovered from your full and final settlement. Whether it is worked out on basic or gross pay depends on your contract.

short: The time you or your employer must give before your employment ends, as set out in your contract.
detail: No law fixes a resignation notice period for private-sector employees, so it comes from your contract, commonly 30 to 90 days. For workers, the IR Code requires one month's notice or pay in lieu before retrenchment.

short: Paying salary in place of the unserved part of a notice period so that an employee can leave early.
detail: The employee or the new employer may pay it, if the current employer agrees. It is a matter of contract, not law.

short: A government-regulated retirement savings scheme that your employer can contribute to as part of your salary.
detail: The employer's contribution can be deducted from taxable salary, within limits, under both tax regimes, which makes it one of the few tax benefits left in the new regime.

short: The share of job offers made that candidates accept.
detail: A low rate usually points to pay, slow decisions or a poor candidate experience.

short: A letter offering you a job, with the role, CTC, joining date and key conditions, which you accept before joining.
detail: It is usually followed by a fuller appointment letter when you join. Check the CTC breakup, notice period, probation and any repayment clauses before you sign.

short: The share of candidates who actually join out of those who accepted an offer.
detail: It matters in India because long notice periods give candidates time to take other offers or counter-offers. Keeping in touch during the notice period helps.

short: A goal-setting method that pairs an ambitious objective with a few measurable key results, usually set each quarter.
detail: OKRs suit setting direction and alignment; many companies keep them separate from ratings and pay.

short: The older way of working out income tax, with higher slab rates but deductions and exemptions such as HRA, LTA and tax-saving investments.
detail: Tell your employer if you want TDS worked out under it, and back your claims with proof. Whether it saves you tax depends on how much you can claim.

short: Helping a new employee settle in and become productive, from joining formalities on day one to the end of the first three months.
detail: It usually includes documents and statutory forms, a buddy, a 30-60-90 day plan and regular check-ins with the manager.

expansion: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020
short: The Labour Code on working hours, annual leave, safety, welfare facilities, contract labour and appointment letters.
detail: It replaced 13 laws, including the Factories Act and the Contract Labour Act. Many of its rules on hours and leave apply to 'workers' in establishments with 10 or more workers.
aliases: Occupational Safety Health and Working Conditions Code

short: Work beyond the normal daily or weekly working hours.
detail: Under the Labour Codes, overtime needs the worker's consent, is capped at a set number of hours a quarter and is paid at twice the ordinary rate of wages.

short: Your 10-character income-tax number, which your employer needs to deduct and report your TDS correctly.
detail: If you do not give your PAN, tax can be deducted at a higher rate, and a wrong PAN means the tax you paid does not show against your name.

short: Leave for a father around the birth or adoption of a child.
detail: No central law requires private employers to give it, so it depends on company policy. Central government employees get 15 days.

short: Paying people fairly and consistently for comparable work, regardless of gender or other personal traits.
detail: HR teams check it by comparing pay for similar roles and levels, then explaining or correcting gaps. Equal pay for the same or similar work is a legal duty under the Code on Wages.

short: The monthly work of calculating each employee's pay, deductions and contributions, paying salaries and filing the related returns.
detail: Under the Code on Wages, monthly wages must be paid by the 7th of the following month. Payroll also feeds the PF, ESI, professional tax and TDS filings.

short: The monthly statement that shows what you earned, what was deducted and what you were paid.
detail: Keep your payslips: banks, landlords and new employers ask for them. Employers must give wage slips under the Labour Code rules, and these can be electronic.

short: Using data about employees, such as hiring, attrition and engagement, to answer business questions and improve decisions.
detail: Start with simple descriptive numbers, protect individuals' privacy and do not read cause into a correlation.

short: A benefit in kind from your employer, such as a company car, housing or stock options, that may be taxed as part of your salary.
detail: Your employer values taxable perks using set rules, adds them to your salary for TDS and lists them in Form 123 (formerly Form 12BA).

short: Any data about a person who can be identified from it, such as a name, phone number, Aadhaar number, salary or medical details.
detail: The DPDP Act covers personal data in digital form, including paper records that are later digitised.

short: Any unauthorised access to, or loss, sharing or destruction of, personal data.
detail: Under the DPDP Act and Rules, the organisation must tell the people affected and the Data Protection Board; this duty applies from May 2027.

short: A written plan that sets specific goals, support and a time frame, often 30 to 90 days, for an employee whose performance is below expectations.
detail: It should follow earlier feedback, not replace it, and its outcome (success, extension or exit) should be recorded fairly. Used only as a route to exit, it damages trust.

short: A gig worker who finds work through an online platform or app, such as a ride-hailing or food-delivery app.
detail: The platform, called an aggregator in the Code on Social Security, must contribute a small share of its turnover towards social security for these workers.

short: The law and workplace rules that protect women from sexual harassment at work and set out how complaints are handled.
detail: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 requires employers to have a policy, run awareness sessions, set up an Internal Committee and file an annual report with the District Officer. Many companies extend their POSH policy to all genders, though the Act itself protects women.

short: Everything between offer acceptance and day one, such as paperwork, equipment and keeping in touch with the new hire.
detail: Good pre-boarding cuts drop-outs during long notice periods and means the new hire can start work on day one.

short: The business that uses contract workers supplied by a contractor.
detail: It shares responsibility for the contract workers' safety and welfare, and if the contractor does not pay their wages it must pay them and recover the amount from the contractor.

short: A trial period after joining, often three to six months, during which the employer assesses your fit before confirming you.
detail: Your appointment letter sets its length and the notice that applies during it. For workers covered by standing orders, the Model Standing Orders, 2026 set probation at six months, extendable by three.

short: A small tax some states charge on salaried people, which your employer deducts from your salary and pays to the state.
detail: The Constitution caps it at ₹2,500 per person a year. Slabs differ by state, and several states, including Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, do not levy it on salaries.

short: A short, frequent survey, often 10 to 15 questions each quarter, to track engagement or a specific issue.
detail: Share results quickly and act on one or two themes, or people stop responding.

short: How well new hires turn out, judged by measures such as performance ratings, early exits and manager feedback after six to twelve months.
Speaking to a candidate's former managers or colleagues to confirm their work history and hear about their performance.
detail: Ask the candidate's permission and whom to contact, and record what referees say in a standard format.

short: Exits of people the organisation wanted to keep, such as high performers or people in critical roles.
detail: It is often a better warning sign than the overall attrition rate.

short: Money your employer pays back, against bills, for expenses you incurred for work, such as travel or a phone bill.
detail: Reimbursements of genuine work expenses backed by bills are not taxable salary, and the Labour Ministry's FAQs say they are not 'wages' under the Labour Codes. Fixed monthly amounts paid without bills are usually taxed as allowances.

short: A letter confirming that you have been released from your job, with your last working day.
detail: New employers usually ask for it. It is common practice rather than a legal requirement, so ask for it in writing if it is delayed.

short: Telling your employer, in writing, that you are leaving your job.
detail: Your notice period runs from the date your contract specifies, usually when the resignation is received or accepted. Under the Code on Wages, wages due must be paid within two working days of your exit.

short: A fund into which an employer pays 15 days' last-drawn wages for each worker it retrenches, to support the worker's reskilling.
detail: The IR Code introduced it, and the money is passed on to the retrenched worker. It is in addition to retrenchment compensation.

short: A holiday you pick from a list of optional festivals, instead of one fixed for everyone.
detail: Your employer decides how many you can take in a year. Central government offices use this system, and many private companies follow it.

short: Keeping the employees you want to keep, and the practices that help, such as good managers, growth and fair pay.
detail: Retention rate is the share of employees at the start of a period who are still there at the end.

short: A payment promised to an employee for staying until a set date, often during a merger, project or restructuring.
detail: It is usually paid only if you are still employed on that date.

short: Payroll shorthand for retirement benefits the employer pays on top of salary, mainly employer PF and gratuity.
detail: They are part of CTC but do not reach you each month, which is one reason in-hand pay is lower than CTC divided by 12.

short: Ending a worker's job for reasons other than discipline, such as surplus staff or restructuring.
detail: Under the IR Code, a worker with a year's service gets one month's notice or pay in lieu, compensation of 15 days' average pay for each completed year, and a payment into the reskilling fund. Factories, mines and plantations with 300 or more workers need government permission first.

short: Total revenue divided by headcount, a rough measure of workforce productivity.
detail: Compare it over time and with companies in the same industry, not across industries.

short: The minimum-to-maximum pay range a company sets for a job level.
detail: The midpoint is the target pay for someone fully competent in the role. Bands keep pay decisions consistent and easier to explain.

short: How your CTC is split into parts such as basic, HRA, allowances, retirals and variable pay.
detail: The split changes your in-hand pay, PF, gratuity and tax. Under the Labour Codes, excluded allowances above half of total pay count as wages, so very low-basic structures no longer cut statutory costs.

short: A leave-policy rule that counts weekends or holidays falling between two leave days as leave too.
detail: For example, leave on Friday and Monday may be counted as four days. No law requires it; it applies only if your company's leave policy says so.

short: The section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 that covers TDS on salary, in place of section 192 of the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026.
detail: Payroll software, Form 130 and the forms employees give their employers, such as Form 122 and Form 124, now refer to it.

short: A payment an employer makes when it ends someone's job, beyond the dues they have already earned.
detail: The law requires retrenchment compensation for workers; anything more is set by the contract or company policy.

short: The Ministry of Women and Child Development's online portal where a woman can file a sexual harassment complaint, which is then sent to the right committee.
detail: Using it does not replace an employer's duty to have its own Internal Committee.

short: A fixed block of working hours, such as morning, evening or night, used where work runs beyond normal office hours.
detail: Women may work night shifts (before 6 am or after 7 pm) only with their consent and with the safety measures, facilities and transport the rules require.

short: A state law that regulates working conditions in shops, offices and other commercial establishments, such as hours, holidays, leave and registration.
detail: Each state has its own Act, and they continue alongside the Labour Codes. Some states have amended theirs since 2025, Karnataka among them in 2026, so check the current version for your state.

short: A written notice asking an employee to explain, by a deadline, why disciplinary action should not be taken for alleged misconduct.
detail: It should state the specific allegations and evidence. It is usually the first step before a domestic inquiry.

short: Paid leave you take when you are ill or injured.
detail: There is no national minimum for private employers; state laws and company policy set it, and a medical certificate is often needed for longer absences. Employees covered by ESI can also claim cash sickness benefit from ESIC.

short: Finding and approaching possible candidates for a role, through job boards, referrals, LinkedIn, agencies or direct outreach.
detail: Track hires and cost by channel, not just applications, to see which sources work for which roles.

short: The number of people who report directly to one manager.
detail: Too narrow adds layers and cost; too wide leaves people without support. The right number depends on how similar and independent the work is.

short: A catch-all allowance that makes up the rest of your fixed salary after basic, HRA and other named parts.
detail: It is not on the Labour Codes' list of exclusions, so it usually counts as 'wages' for PF, gratuity and bonus. It is fully taxable.

short: A flat amount taken off your salary income before tax is worked out, with no proof needed.
detail: It applies under both tax regimes, but the amount is different in each.

short: Written rules of employment, covering matters such as shifts, leave, misconduct and termination, that larger industrial employers must have.
detail: Under the IR Code they are required where 300 or more workers are employed. Employers can adopt the government's Model Standing Orders, 2026 for manufacturing, mining or services.

short: A way to answer, or assess answers to, behavioural interview questions by describing a real situation, your task, what you did and the result.
detail: Interviewers listen for the candidate's own actions ('I', not 'we') and a measurable result.

short: A yearly bonus the law requires for employees whose wages are within a limit set by the government.
detail: Under the Code on Wages it is at least {{fact:bonus.minRate}} of wages (or ₹100, if higher) and at most {{fact:bonus.maxRate}}, and you qualify after working at least 30 days in the accounting year. It is separate from any performance bonus your company pays.

short: The records of attendance, wages, leave, overtime and other details that labour laws require employers to keep.
detail: The Labour Codes allow registers, records and returns to be kept and filed electronically. Inspectors can ask to see them.

short: A one-to-one conversation with a current employee about what keeps them and what might make them leave.
detail: Managers usually hold them with key people once or twice a year and act on what they hear.

short: Workers stopping work together to press their demands.
detail: Under the IR Code, workers in any industrial establishment must give notice within 60 days before a strike and can't strike within 14 days of giving it. Half or more of the workers taking casual leave together on the same day counts as a strike.

short: An interview in which every candidate for a role is asked the same questions and scored against the same rubric.
detail: Research finds structured interviews predict job performance better than free-form chats. Interviewers should score on their own before they discuss.

short: A plan naming who could step into each critical role, and how soon, if the current holder leaves.
detail: Review it at least once a year and give each named successor a development plan.

short: Retiring on reaching the retirement age set by your employer, often 58 or 60.
detail: Gratuity is payable on superannuation. The word is also used for a superannuation fund, a retirement benefit some employers offer.

expansion: Tax deduction and collection account number
short: The employer's registration number for deducting and depositing TDS; it appears on your Form 16, or Form 130 from tax year 2026-27.
The 12-month period from 1 April to 31 March for which income is taxed under the Income-tax Act, 2025.
detail: It replaced the old pair of 'previous year' and 'assessment year' from 1 April 2026, so income earned in 2026-27 is taxed for tax year 2026-27. Income up to 31 March 2026 is still dealt with under the 1961 Act.

short: Income tax your employer cuts from your salary every month and pays to the government on your behalf.
detail: The employer estimates your tax for the whole tax year under the regime you choose and spreads it over the remaining months. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, TDS on salary falls under section 392.

short: The employer ending your employment, for reasons such as misconduct, poor performance or the end of a contract.
detail: The employer should follow the contract, any standing orders and a fair process, such as a show-cause notice and inquiry for misconduct. Wages due must still be paid within two working days.

short: How long it takes to hire, counted in days up to the point an offer is accepted.
detail: Time to fill usually counts from when the job is approved or posted; time to hire counts from when the chosen candidate entered the process. Say which one you use.

short: Your 12-digit PF number that stays the same across every job, so all your PF accounts sit under one number.
detail: Give it to each new employer instead of getting a new one, and link it with Aadhaar and your bank account on the EPFO member portal so transfers and withdrawals go through.

short: The part of your pay that depends on your own, your team's or the company's performance, usually paid yearly or quarterly.
detail: Offers often include 'target' variable pay in CTC, but the actual payout can be lower or higher. The Labour Ministry's FAQs say performance-linked variable pay is not 'wages' under the Labour Codes.

short: Extra PF you choose to contribute from your salary above the compulsory share; your employer does not have to match it.
detail: It earns the same interest rate as your EPF balance. Ask payroll to set it up.

short: Under the Labour Codes, the part of your pay used to work out PF, gratuity, bonus and other dues.
detail: It starts from all your pay and leaves out a fixed list of items, such as HRA, conveyance, overtime, commission and the employer's PF share. If those left-out items add up to more than half of your total pay, the excess is counted back in as wages.

short: Your rest day each week, usually Sunday.
detail: Under the OSH Code, a worker may not be made to work more than six days a week, and a substitute rest day is due if the weekly off is taken away.

short: An arrangement to do your job from home or another place away from the office, fully or on some days.
detail: The Model Standing Orders, 2026 for the services sector are reported to allow it by agreement between employer and employee; check the notified text. A clear policy should cover hours, data security and equipment.

short: In the Labour Codes, an employee doing manual, technical, clerical or similar work, as distinct from a manager.
detail: It leaves out people employed mainly in managerial or administrative roles and supervisors earning more than ₹18,000 a month. Many protections, such as standing orders, retrenchment rules and some hours and leave rules, apply only to workers.

short: Working out how many people, with what skills, the organisation will need, and how to get them through hiring, development or other options.
The hours you are expected to work each day and week, within limits set by law.
detail: Under the OSH Code, a worker may be required to work no more than 8 hours a day and 48 hours a week, and work beyond that is paid as overtime. State Shops and Establishments Acts may set different limits for shops and offices.
